content_voiceover: This figure links von Willebrand factor, factor eight, and platelets across three panels. At baseline, VWF multimers circulate coiled up, with factor eight bound to the N-terminus of VWF, and that binding is what protects factor eight from rapid proteolytic clearance, essentially giving it a longer half-life. With vessel injury, VWF adheres to the exposed subendothelial matrix. Under high shear stress, those VWF multimers uncoil, exposing binding sites that let platelets adhere and become activated. Activated platelets then flip phosphatidylserine to their outer membrane surface, creating a procoagulant surface that recruits and concentrates factor eight, setting up the tenase complex for the coagulation cascade. The end result is bleeding cessation by a combined platelet-fibrin plug, followed by thrombolysis and tissue repair. High-yield point for boards, because factor eight rides on VWF, von Willebrand disease can present with a secondarily low factor eight level, which sometimes mimics mild hemophilia A on initial workup.
keypoints: VWF binds and protects FVIII (N-terminus) → prolongs FVIII half-life
High shear uncoils VWF multimers → exposes platelet-binding site
Activated platelets expose phosphatidylserine → procoagulant surface
VWD can present with low FVIII, mimicking hemophilia A
keypoint_voiceover: The key testable fact here is that VWF is a carrier protein for factor eight, protecting it from clearance. So in von Willebrand disease, factor eight levels can be secondarily low, which can look like hemophilia A on initial labs. Also remember that shear-induced unfolding of VWF multimers is what exposes the platelet-binding site, and activated platelets expose phosphatidylserine to support the coagulation cascade.
